summary:
Mayotte stands under France's national framework. Identity documents, criminal law, the anti-discrimination statute and the marriage regime apply here as they do in metropolitan France, and the French prison rules bind the island's places of deprivation of liberty as French establishments.

Nothing in that framework criminalises being trans or being in a same-sex relationship. Same-sex marriage has been available on the island since Mayotte voted to remain part of France in 1975, and it is one of the few jurisdictions in Africa and the Muslim-majority world where such marriages can be performed. The National Assembly's vote simplifying legal gender change for trans people likewise extends to the department.

Placement in custody follows the gender marker carried on the identity document, under Article D248 of the French criminal procedure code. Trans women are therefore typically held in all-male facilities, where other detainees threaten them; anatomy does not decide where a person is placed.

The national detention-places watchdog CGLPL reported on 25 May 2021 a persistence of serious violations of transgender detainees' fundamental rights across all French places of deprivation of liberty. The finding rests on referrals made since 2010 concerning some forty transgender people and on site inspections at which eight trans women and one trans man were interviewed, at Fleury-Mérogis, Caen, Saint-Martin-de-Ré and Toulouse. Because these are French establishments, the same standards and the same documented failures govern any facility holding a trans person on Mayotte.

Formal entitlement and lived experience diverge on the island. A teacher at the university centre of Mayotte and his Malagasy partner married at Sada town hall in 2023 only after what reporting described as a long and complicated path, on a predominantly Muslim island where the law on paper is not the whole of what a couple faces.

Legal representation is thinly available locally. A French-language directory of LGBT-friendly lawyers returns no referenced practitioner for Mayotte's towns, including Mamoudzou, Koungou, Dzaoudzi and Sada, while listing a Paris-based lawyer admitted to the Conseil d'État and Cour de cassation, working in persons and family law, as available.
tangentialFactors:
French law has barred discrimination on grounds of gender identity since article 225-1 of the Penal Code was amended on 18 November 2016, replacing the earlier wording of 'sexual identity'; the Labour Code separately prohibits exclusion from recruitment, internships or training, and sanction, dismissal or discriminatory measures, on account of gender identity.

Legal gender change without surgery, forced sterilisation, psychiatric certification or proof of medical intervention took effect on 1 January 2017, though the gender marker still requires an application to a court, while a first-name change can be made at the registry office. Transphobia has been an aggravating factor for all crimes punishable by imprisonment since 2017.

A report of 16 May 2020 recorded a 36% rise in homophobic and transphobic attacks and insults in 2019, with around 1,870 victims identified by police against around 1,380 in 2018. These are national figures and no Mayotte-specific breakdown was sourced.

Healthcare provision was found by a 2022 ILGA-Europe report to suffer from lack of self-determination, extended waiting times and inequitable access by location. In March 2024 centre-right senators commissioned a report critical of youth gender-affirming care, after which legislation to ban medical transition under age 18 passed the Senate in May 2024 but is opposed by the government, with no update since 23 July 2024.
localsOnly:
Transgender people are permitted to serve openly in the French Armed Forces, and conversion therapy was banned by Senate vote of 7 December 2020, National Assembly concurrence on 25 January 2022 and publication on 1 February 2022, carrying proposed punishments of two years' imprisonment and a fine of 30,000 euros.

In March 2019 the Minister of Higher Education sought use of transgender people's preferred names on student cards and exam forms, a measure that reaches the university centre of Mayotte as a French institution.

Transsexualism remains classified under ALD 31, with treatment funded by the Sécurité Sociale, and gender-affirming surgery performed in France was legalised in 1979 after previously being accessible only abroad. France removed gender identity disorder as a diagnosis by decree in 2010, though transgender rights organisations stated at the time that nothing changed beyond the announcement.

Same-sex marriage is legal in all overseas departments and territories under French law; when the 2013 marriage equality bill was voted, 11 of 27 overseas deputies voted for, 11 against, 1 abstained and 3 were absent.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Mayotte-specific incident of violence against a trans person, and no local enforcement record of the hate-crime aggravating factor, was identified in the sources; the attack statistics cited are national and undifferentiated by territory.

Whether any facility on Mayotte currently holds a trans detainee, and how Article D248 placement has operated in practice at the island's places of deprivation of liberty, is not sourced here.

The gap between formal rights and lived experience on the island rests on a single documented marriage case from 2023; a broader measure of local attitudes or administrative obstruction is not available.

The status of the Senate-passed bill to ban medical transition under age 18 remains unresolved as of the last sourced update of 23 July 2024, and its application to Mayotte is not separately documented.
